paras: The lynching of Joseph E. Jenkins and Eugene Azar took place on May 15, 1882, when a crowd of about 200 to 300 men took Jenkins, a white man held on a murder charge, from the parish jail at St. Martinsville, Louisiana, and hanged him near Breaux Bridge, together with Azar, a Black man seized on the way. Governor S. D. McEnery offered a $2,000 reward, and sixteen men were later jailed, but a St. Martin Parish grand jury returned no true bill and the prisoners were released. Papers across the country noted that the second victim, out on bond on a lesser or disputed charge, had simply been met on the road, and later dispatches reported armed Black residents swearing vengeance.

About a week before the lynching, Jenkins shot and killed his brother-in-law Raphael Castille near Breaux Bridge, in what one wire said he claimed was a case of mistaken identity. He was arrested on an affidavit by the coroner, Dr. A. Guilbeau, and held in the parish jail at St. Martinsville to await trial. Azar, described as a young Black man, was then free on bond after being charged with killing a young man raised by Valery Thibodeaux; one report said an inquest had found the killing to be self-defence and set his bail at $300.

On the morning of Monday, May 15, while Sheriff U. A. Guilbeau was away on his plantation, about 200 men on horseback surrounded the parish prison. Col. Deblanc tried to dissuade them, but the sheriff's young son, acting as jailor, saw resistance was vain and threw away the key; the crowd let Jenkins receive the last rites of the Church and rode with him toward Breaux Bridge.

On the way the crowd seized Azar, and at about 4 p.m. both men were hanged from one tree about half a mile from Breaux Bridge, near the place where Castille had been killed. The St. Landry Democrat said the hanging took place in the presence of Jenkins's wife, and later specials said she begged for his life and that the crowd broke Jenkins's arms with clubs when he grasped the rope.

Sheriff Guilbeau telegraphed the governor on May 15 and 16 that 'the people of the parish are outraged', and McEnery answered that he had offered $2,000 for the arrest and conviction of those who hanged the two men. By May 25 sixteen men had been arrested, though local papers gave eleven or twelve. At a preliminary examination before Judge Theodore Fontelieu that began on May 23 and lasted two days, bail was refused and the accused were returned to jail.

Dispatches from Baton Rouge and New Orleans described a 'reign of terror' in the parish, with bands of armed Black men in St. Martinsville swearing vengeance for Azar's death and a clash feared. At a special term of court that opened on July 18, the grand jury endorsed the bill in State vs Thibodeaux et als 'Not a true bill', and the prisoners were freed and went home the same day.

Outside Louisiana the lynching appeared mostly as one-paragraph wire items on May 17 and 18, headed 'Lynched', 'Double Lynching' or 'Lynch Law in Louisiana', and the earliest briefs mentioned only Jenkins. The wires mangled the names, printing Azar as Azor, Ascor, Azas and Ayrose, and Castille as William Castello; one Dallas item even raised the reward to $20,000. A few distant papers commented: the San Antonio Evening Light called the hangings 'acts of gross murder', and the Nevada Silver State called Azar's death 'a hideous piece of atrocity'.

Louisiana papers were divided: the Lafayette Advertiser called it 'one of the worst cases of the kind in our State's history', and the St. Landry Democrat called it a 'double murder' whose perpetrators should be punished. The Iberia Star, reprinted by the Thibodaux Sentinel, reported that the mob told the authorities no reward was needed because they were 'citizens of good standing', and the Sentinel blamed 'the modern jury system'. The St. Martin Observer protested 'in the name of civilisation' but held the parish authorities 'morally responsible', and a St. Martinsville correspondent signing himself 'Vindex' blamed juries 'composed of ignorant negroes' and called the lynchers 'more deserving of pity than blame'.
Later wire stories shifted attention to Azar and to Black anger, under headlines such as 'Arrested for Lynching the Wrong Man' and 'Armed Negroes Swearing Vengeance in Louisiana'.

Sheriff Guilbeau's telegrams place the jail raid at about 11 a.m. and the hanging at about 4 p.m. on May 15, while wire versions gave 'early yesterday morning', 'Monday night', or Tuesday, May 16, and 'Vindex' gave 'the 13th instant'. The Associated Press called the crowd 'a mob of whites and blacks', but the Times-Star described 'a mob of white men'.

Accounts of Azar differ most: the Times-Democrat said he had killed a young man in January, the Telegram said an inquest found self-defence, the Times-Star said the death followed a horse collision on a road, and a New Orleans wire said he was out on bail for petty larceny; the AP said he protested his innocence.

reader.title: Lynching of Joseph E. Jenkins and Eugene Azar
bases: A crowd of 200 to 300 men took Jenkins from the St. Martinsville jail, seized Azar, who was out on bond, and hanged both on one tree near Breaux Bridge (A18, A16, A40).

Both men were hanged without trial by a crowd of 200 to 500 that took Jenkins from jail on a murder charge and Azar while he was out on bond on a homicide charge (A18, A4, A39); local defenders justified it by the failure of the courts and juries (A38, A31, A40).
The sheriff's telegrams (A18), independent local reports (A16, A19, A40) and several wire services (A4, A10, A13) agree that both men were taken and hanged on one tree near Breaux Bridge.

accounts.label: Sheriff's telegrams
accounts.gist: A crowd of 200 raided the jail about 11 a.m. on May 15 in the sheriff's absence; Jenkins was hanged at Breaux Bridge about 4 p.m., and Azar, seized on the way, was hanged on the same tree.

accounts.label: St. Martin Observer (local)
accounts.gist: About 200 horsemen surrounded the prison; the sheriff's son threw away the key; Jenkins received last rites and was hanged about 4 p.m. near the scene of the killing, with Azor seized on the way.

accounts.label: Times-Democrat special
accounts.gist: 300 men took Jenkins from jail to the place of the murder near Breaux Bridge; on the way they came across Azar, who had killed a young man in January, and hanged him on the same tree.

accounts.label: Associated Press (Baton Rouge)
accounts.gist: A mob 'of whites and blacks' attacked the jail early in the morning, hanged Jenkins, then hunted up James Azor, out on bail for murdering a young white man, and hanged him despite his protests of innocence.

accounts.label: Times-Star and Telegram specials
accounts.gist: A mob of white men hanged Jenkins (white) and Ayroz (colored); Ayroz's offence was slight and he was out on $300 bail; Jenkins's arms were broken with clubs; armed Black men swore vengeance.

framing.detail: The Lafayette Advertiser called it a 'Terrible Tragedy' in which 'unauthorized and unjustified violence held full sway'.
The St. Landry Democrat called it a 'double murder' and said the jailed men should be punished.
The Iberia Star and Thibodaux Sentinel blamed the jury system and said such deeds would continue until justice was better administered.
The St. Martin Observer protested the act 'in the name of civilisation' but hesitated to blame the people and held the authorities morally responsible.
'Vindex' blamed juries 'composed of ignorant negroes' and called the lynchers 'more deserving of pity than blame'.
Most out-of-state papers ran one-paragraph wire briefs headed 'Lynched', 'Double Lynching' or 'Lynch Law in Louisiana'.
The San Antonio Evening Light and the Nevada Silver State called the hangings 'gross murder' and 'a hideous piece of atrocity'.
Later wires headed 'A Reign of Terror' and 'Armed Negroes Swearing Vengeance' put Black residents' anger at the center.

conflicts.note: The sheriff's telegrams dated May 15 and 16 are the best evidence and fix the hanging at about 4 p.m. on Monday, May 15; the May 16 dates come from wires that said 'yesterday' a day late.

info: Monday, May 15, 1882: the sheriff telegraphed that day that the jail was raided about 11 a.m., and the next day that Jenkins 'was hung about 4 p.m. yesterday'; local papers say 'last Monday'. Wire versions give May 16 or Tuesday, and one letter gives 'the 13th instant'.
Taken from the parish jail at St. Martinsville; hanged on a tree near Breaux Bridge, about half a mile from town, at or near the place where Castille was killed.
Joseph E. Jenkins, called 'a white man', and Eugene Azar (also printed Azor, Ascor, Azas, Ayrose, Ayroz; first name James in the AP wire), called colored or a negro.

Jenkins was held on a charge of shooting and killing his brother-in-law Raphael Castille. Azar was out on bond on a charge of killing a young man; other reports say an inquest had found self-defence, that the death came from a horse collision, or that his charge was petty larceny.
Men from around Breaux Bridge; those arrested were prosecuted as 'State vs Thibodeaux et als'. The AP wire said 'whites and blacks'; a Times-Star special said 'a mob of white men'.
The prisoners were discharged by the court and went home the same day.
